name: Vocal cord and pharyngeal distal myopathy (MATR3)
aliases: distal myopathy with vocal cord and pharyngeal weakness

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant adult-onset distal myopathy caused by variants in MATR3, which encodes the nuclear matrix RNA/DNA-binding protein matrin-3
Distinctive for combining distal limb weakness with bulbar features, namely vocal cord weakness causing dysphonia and a nasal voice, and pharyngeal weakness causing dysphagia
Distal weakness typically begins in the hands and feet and progresses slowly, sometimes later extending proximally
Onset is usually in adulthood, often in the fourth to sixth decade
The same MATR3 gene is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia, so a mixed motor-neuron/myopathic picture can occur and warrants careful evaluation
Respiratory muscle involvement can develop and is an important cause of morbidity, so ventilatory function should be monitored
Creatine kinase is normal or mildly raised; electromyography shows myopathic changes that may coexist with features suggesting neurogenic involvement
Diagnosis relies on the characteristic distal-plus-bulbar phenotype confirmed by MATR3 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is caused by dominant variants in MATR3, encoding matrin-3, an RNA- and DNA-binding protein of the nuclear matrix involved in RNA processing, stability, and transport. Disease-associated variants alter matrin-3 handling of RNA and its protein interactions, leading to abnormal protein accumulation and dysfunction in muscle and, in some individuals, motor neurons. This shared molecular biology explains the overlap with motor neuron disease. In muscle the process causes a distal myopathy with particular vulnerability of laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, producing the characteristic vocal cord and swallowing involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with bulbar involvement
Myasthenia gravis with bulbar and limb weakness
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise myopathic and any neurogenic features
Laryngoscopy and swallowing assessment for vocal cord and pharyngeal weakness
Respiratory function testing including lying and sitting vital capacity
Muscle biopsy where indicated, which may show rimmed vacuoles and myopathic changes
Targeted MATR3 sequencing or a distal myopathy/motor neuron disease gene panel
redFlags: Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk or weight loss
Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation
Features of motor neuron disease such as fasciculations, brisk reflexes, or bulbar wasting
Rapid deterioration atypical for a slowly progressive distal myopathy
Stridor or airway compromise from vocal cord dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Limb weakness usually progresses slowly, but bulbar and respiratory involvement can significantly affect quality of life and survival; prognosis is worse if the phenotype overlaps with motor neuron disease, making swallowing and respiratory surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Mistaking the bulbar features for oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy or myasthenia gravis
Overlooking respiratory muscle weakness and aspiration risk
Missing an overlapping motor neuron disease phenotype linked to MATR3
Attributing dysphonia solely to a laryngeal cause without recognising the underlying myopathy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Supportive multidisciplinary neuromuscular care, as no disease-specific or curative therapy exists
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids for progressive distal weakness
Swallowing assessment and dysphagia management with dietary modification, considering gastrostomy if pharyngeal weakness is severe
Voice and communication support for dysphonia from vocal cord weakness
Respiratory surveillance with lying and sitting vital capacity, introducing non-invasive ventilation as respiratory muscles fail
Monitor for overlap with motor neuron disease, warranting careful neurological evaluation
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
